planting.note: Plant bulb offsets in spring, 4–6 inches deep, into humus-rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; woodland spider lily is native to bottomland woods and shaded stream terraces and needs shade rather than full sun to perform well.

directions: Plant bulbs in humus-rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; woodland spider lily is a true forest-floor native, found wild in bottomland hardwood forests and along shaded stream terraces across the southeastern and south-central United States. Strap-like leaves emerge in spring, followed in late summer by clusters of fragrant, spidery white flowers with narrow, curving petals surrounding a central cup, held on tall, leafless stalks above the foliage. It multiplies slowly by offsets into a modest colony over the years and is one of relatively few bulbs that genuinely thrive in deep or dappled shade rather than merely tolerating it, making it valuable for woodland gardens, shaded borders, and naturalistic plantings under deciduous trees. Leave the foliage in place after bloom to recharge the bulb for next year, and divide congested clumps only when flowering noticeably declines, since it resents frequent disturbance.

planting.note: Plant bulb offsets in spring into rich, humus-heavy, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Amazon lily is a true tropical understory plant that scorches in direct sun and is best grown in a shaded bed or large container in all but the mildest frost-free climates.

directions: Plant in rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Amazon lily is a South American rainforest understory bulb with broad, glossy, dark green leaves and clusters of large, fragrant, pure white, daffodil-like flowers that can appear more than once a year in warm, humid conditions rather than on a single fixed bloom schedule. It genuinely requires shade, humidity, and consistent moisture to thrive, making it a poor fit for typical sunny bulb borders but an excellent choice for a shaded lanai, greenhouse, or humid understory planting in the tropics. Outside true frost-free zones, grow it as a container specimen that summers outdoors in shade and moves to a warm, bright indoor spot before any hint of frost, since even light chilling can damage or kill the bulb. Repot or divide crowded clumps only when flowering declines, as Amazon lily blooms best when slightly pot-bound.

planting.note: Plant bulb offsets with the neck at or just above soil level into well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade; Barbados lily is the wild species behind many hybrid amaryllis and naturalizes readily and persistently in Gulf Coast and Florida gardens.

directions: Plant bulbs with the neck at or just above soil level in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Barbados lily is a wild, naturalized amaryllis species long established around old homesteads and cemeteries throughout the Gulf South and Florida, sending up tall, leafless stalks topped with two to four trumpet-shaped, orange-red flowers in spring, smaller and more numerous per stalk than showy hybrid amaryllis. Strap-like leaves follow the flowers and persist through summer before dying back for a winter dormancy in cooler parts of its range, though it stays evergreen in essentially frost-free gardens. It is tougher and considerably more heat- and humidity-tolerant than most florist hybrid amaryllis, multiplying steadily by offsets into substantial naturalized clumps that can persist and rebloom for decades with virtually no care. Leave clumps undisturbed for the best flowering, dividing only when a planting becomes overcrowded and bloom noticeably declines.

planting.note: Plant bulb offsets 2 inches deep after last frost once soil has warmed, into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; tuberose needs a long, hot summer to bloom well and should be dug and stored indoors over winter outside its hardiness range.

directions: Plant bulbs in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after the soil has thoroughly warmed; tuberose sends up grass-like leaves through summer followed by tall, sturdy flower spikes in late summer to fall, densely packed with waxy white blooms carrying one of the most intensely sweet, heady fragrances of any garden flower, especially pronounced after dusk. It is a favorite for cut flower arrangements, bridal bouquets, and fragrance gardens, and the classic double-flowered 'The Pearl' selection is widely grown for its extra-full blooms. In zone 8, bulbs can often be left in the ground with heavy winter mulch, but in colder climates dig clumps after the foliage yellows in fall, cure them, and store in a cool, dry, frost-free spot for replanting the following spring. Feed lightly through the growing season and keep soil evenly moist, since inconsistent watering during bud formation can cause flower spikes to blast or fail to open fully.
